title: Ginseng
description: Root of a plant used in herbal preparations
wiki_lead:
Ginseng () is the root of plants in the genus Panax, such as South China ginseng (P. notoginseng), Korean ginseng (P. ginseng), and American ginseng (P. quinquefolius), characterized by the presence of ginsenosides and gintonin.
Ginseng has been used in the traditional medicine of Korea and China for centuries, although there is no clinical evidence that it has any therapeutic effects. There is no substantial evidence that ginseng is effective for treating any medical condition and it has not been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to treat or prevent a disease or to provide a health benefit. Although ginseng is sold as a dietary supplement, inconsistent manufacturing practices for supplements have led to analyses of some ginseng products contaminated with unrelated filler compounds, and its excessive use may have adverse effects or untoward interactions with prescription drugs.

Although ginseng is sold as a dietary supplement, inconsistent manufacturing practices for supplements have led to analyses of some ginseng products contaminated with unrelated filler compounds, and its excessive use may have adverse effects or untoward interactions with prescription drugs.


Etymology
The English word "ginseng" comes from the Teochew Chinese jîn-sim (人蔘; where this transliteration is in Pe̍h-ōe-jī). The first character 人 (pinyin rén; Modern Standard Mandarin pronunciation: [ʐə̌n] or [ɻə̌n]) means "person" and the second character 蔘 (pinyin: shēn; MSM: [ʂə́n]) means "plant root" in a forked shape.


Ginseng species


Genus
Ginseng plants belong only to the genus Panax. Cultivated species include Panax ginseng (Korean ginseng), Panax japonicus (Japanese ginseng), Panax notoginseng (South China ginseng), Panax quinquefolius (American ginseng). Ginseng is found in cooler climates – the Korean Peninsula, Northeast China, Russian Far East, Canada and the United States, although some species grow in warm regions – South China ginseng being native to Southwest China and Vietnam. Panax vietnamensis (Vietnamese ginseng) is the southernmost Panax species known.


Wild ginseng

Wild ginseng (Korean: 산삼; Hanja: 山蔘; RR: sansam; lit. 'mountain ginseng') grows naturally in mountains and is hand-picked by gatherers known as simmani (심마니). The wild ginseng plant is almost extinct in China and endangered globally. This is due to high demand for the product in recent years, leading to the harvesting of wild plants faster than they can grow and reproduce (a wild ginseng plant can take years to reach maturity). Wild ginseng can be processed to be red or white ginseng.
Wild American ginseng has long been used by Native Americans for medicine. Since the mid-1700s, it has been harvested for international trade. Wild American ginseng can be harvested in 19 states and the Appalachian Mountains but has restrictions for exporting.


Cultivated ginseng

Cultivated ginseng (Korean: 인삼; Hanja: 人蔘; RR: insam; lit. 'human ginseng') is less expensive than the rarely available wild ginseng.
Cultivated ginseng (Korean: 장뇌삼; Hanja: 長腦蔘; RR: jangnoesam) is planted on mountains by humans and is allowed to grow like wild ginseng.


Other plants sometimes called ginseng
True ginseng plants belong only to the genus Panax. Several other plants are sometimes referred to as ginseng, but they are from a different genus or even family. Siberian ginseng is in the same family, but not genus, as true ginseng. The active compounds in Siberian ginseng are eleutherosides, not ginsenosides. Instead of a fleshy root, Siberian ginseng has a woody root.

grok_lead: Ginseng refers to several slow-growing perennial plants in the genus Panax of the family Araliaceae, primarily Panax ginseng (Asian or Korean ginseng) native to East Asia and Panax quinquefolius (American ginseng) native to the deciduous forests of eastern North America, prized for their fleshy roots used in traditional medicine as a tonic and adaptogen. The roots, which resemble the shape of a human figureâhence the name derived from the Chinese rÃ©nshÄn meaning "man root"âcontain bioactive compounds known as ginsenosides, triterpenoid saponins that are responsible for many of the plant's pharmacological effects. Botanically, these herbaceous plants typically grow 20-70 cm tall with palmately compound leaves featuring 3-5 ovate leaflets, producing small greenish-white flowers in umbels followed by red berries containing 1-3 seeds, and requiring shaded, moist woodland conditions to thrive over 3-6 years before harvest. With a history spanning over 5,000 years, ginseng has been documented in ancient Chinese texts such as Shen Nong's Pharmacopoeia (c. 196 AD) as a superior tonic for vitality, longevity, and treating ailments like fatigue and digestive issues, initially reserved for emperors before spreading through trade to Korea, Japan, and beyond. In Korea, cultivation began around 11 B.C., and by the 12th century, red ginsengâproduced by steaming the rootsâwas established as a key preparation for enhancing immunity and energy, while American ginseng was discovered by European explorers in the 18th century and exported to Asia for similar uses. Today, ginseng is cultivated commercially in regions like Wisconsin for American varieties and South Korea for Asian ones, with global demand driving conservation efforts due to overharvesting of wild populations, which are now protected under CITES for American ginseng. Medicinally, ginseng is renowned for its adaptogenic properties, helping the body resist stress and restore balance, with scientific studies supporting benefits such as improved immune function through enhanced antibody production, reduced blood glucose in type 2 diabetes patients, and potential anticancer effects via ginsenosides like Rg3 that inhibit tumor growth. Active components include over 40 ginsenosides (e.g., Rb1 for neuroprotection and Rg1 for cognitive enhancement), polysaccharides for immune modulation, and polyacetylenes with antimicrobial activity, though efficacy varies by preparation (white vs. red ginseng) and individual response, with ongoing research emphasizing standardized extracts for clinical use. Despite its popularity in supplements, teas, and tonics worldwide, ginseng is not without risks, including interactions with medications and side effects like insomnia, underscoring the need for evidence-based application in modern herbal therapy.
